---
title: International review and localization
description: A repeatable review protocol for multi-country NADABAS documentation.
---

::: {.callout-important title="Scope"}
This guide makes a technical review package easier to assess across countries
and languages. It does not establish legal compliance, certification, or
approval by the African Union, European Union, ASEAN, a member state, or a
national institution.
:::

## Review principles

1. **Use one traceable technical baseline.** Every review identifies a Git
   commit, documentation version, deployment profile, and review date.
2. **Separate fact from proposal.** Mark statements as source-verified,
   environment-dependent, legacy-draft, or unknown.
3. **Review by concern and role.** Technical, domain, database, security,
   operations, accessibility, and localization reviewers sign off only on their
   scope.
4. **Keep English plain and translation-ready.** Define terms, avoid idioms,
   keep sentences focused, and separate translatable prose from identifiers.
5. **Record national differences explicitly.** Do not hide a jurisdiction,
   language, infrastructure, or operating-model difference in a generic
   regional statement.
6. **Preserve every disposition.** Accepted, rejected, deferred, and superseded
   comments remain traceable to evidence and a decision.

These principles are informed by
[ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022](https://www.iso.org/standard/74393.html),
[ISO/IEC/IEEE 42030:2019](https://www.iso.org/standard/73436.html), the
[ISO plain-language principles](https://www.iso.org/standard/78907.html), and
the [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/).
They are guidance for this project, not a claim of standards conformance.

## Language and translation policy

The English repository version is the normative technical working version
unless a release explicitly designates another authoritative version.

| Translation status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Normative working version** | The version against which technical changes and review dispositions are recorded. |
| **Reviewed translation** | A human reviewer has checked the translation against an identified source commit and terminology set. |
| **Assisted translation** | Machine or computer-assisted output awaiting human review; it is informative only. |
| **Superseded translation** | A translation whose source version has changed; keep it for provenance but do not use it for current decisions. |

Every translated artifact must record:

- document identifier and title;
- source commit and source-language version;
- language using a valid [BCP 47 language
  tag](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/html/H57.html);
- translation status, translator or service, and human reviewer;
- review date and known untranslated or disputed terms.

Code identifiers, VBA names, SQL identifiers, file names, registry keys, command
names, and claim IDs stay unchanged. Translate their explanation, not the
identifier.

## Review package

Prepare a small, self-contained package rather than asking reviewers to infer
context from the repository.

| Item | Required content |
|---|---|
| Cover note | Purpose, decision requested, owner, deadline, and contact point. |
| Baseline | Repository URL, commit, branch or release, documentation version, and generated-output checksum when distributed outside GitHub. |
| Scope | Included components, deployment profile, languages, jurisdictions, and explicit exclusions. |
| Architecture | Context and component views, data flows, trust boundaries, and claim IDs. |
| Evidence register | Source or test evidence for every material architecture claim. |
| Risk and decision log | Security findings, known unknowns, deferred work, and relevant ADRs. |
| Terminology set | Approved English terms, acronyms, definitions, non-translatable identifiers, and disputed translations. |
| Review form | Reviewer role, context, comments, outcome, limitations, and sign-off. |

## Reviewer roles

One person may hold several roles, but the review record must state which role
was exercised.

| Role | Questions to answer |
|---|---|
| Domain reviewer | Does the behaviour and terminology match national accounts practice in the reviewed context? |
| Technical reviewer | Are components, interfaces, states, and dependencies accurate and maintainable? |
| Database reviewer | Are products, schemas, permissions, transactions, backup, restore, and migration assumptions correct? |
| Security and privacy reviewer | Are data classifications, credentials, logs, privileges, transfers, retention, and trust boundaries acceptable? |
| Operations reviewer | Can the solution be installed, configured, monitored, recovered, and supported locally? |
| Accessibility reviewer | Can the documentation and relevant interface be used with required assistive technologies and input methods? |
| Localization reviewer | Are language, terminology, character handling, layout, formats, and cultural assumptions appropriate? |
| Governance reviewer | Is the decision owner identified and is the evidence sufficient for the stated decision? |

## Comment format and deferred findings

Use one comment per issue. A recommended identifier is
`IR-<review-code>-<sequence>`, for example `IR-EU-SEC-004`. The identifier does
not imply endorsement by the named region.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Claim or section | Architecture claim ID, heading, file, or line. |
| Category | Accuracy, domain, security/privacy, interoperability, accessibility, localization, operations, governance, or editorial. |
| Severity | Blocking, major, minor, or editorial. |
| Context | Country or organization, deployment type, database type, Office version, and language where relevant. |
| Finding | One observable problem, ambiguity, or missing decision. |
| Evidence | Source, test result, policy, standard, or operational experience supporting the finding. |
| Proposed disposition | Change, accept with rationale, defer to an issue and owner, or reject with rationale. |

A deferred finding is not closed merely by labelling it “fix later.” Record an
owner, target milestone, risk acceptance authority, and the condition that will
trigger re-evaluation. Security, data-integrity, legal, or accessibility blockers
need explicit acceptance by the accountable role; a documentation editor cannot
accept them alone.

## Review workflow

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  prepare["Prepare baseline and review package"] --> screen["Completeness and terminology screen"]
  screen --> review["Independent role-based review"]
  review --> triage["Triage and assign dispositions"]
  triage --> revise["Revise source, evidence, and decisions"]
  revise --> verify["Reviewer verifies resolved findings"]
  verify --> translate["Synchronize reviewed translations"]
  translate --> accept["Record scoped acceptance"]
  accept --> archive["Archive package and provenance"]
```

**Diagram description.** A review starts from a versioned package, proceeds
through independent role-based assessment, and records dispositions before
translations are synchronized. Acceptance is scoped and the full provenance is
retained.

### Acceptance outcomes

- **Accepted for stated scope:** evidence is sufficient for the named version,
  deployment, role, and decision.
- **Accepted with conditions:** named actions have owners, dates, and explicit
  risk acceptance.
- **Revision required:** blocking findings prevent the requested decision.
- **Not assessed:** the reviewer lacked evidence, authority, environment, or
  subject-matter coverage. This is not a negative decision.

## Translation-ready authoring rules

- Use UTF-8/Unicode throughout source and generated web content.
- Declare the page language and identify passages in another language; WCAG 2.2
  addresses both language of page and language of parts.
- Use approved terms consistently and expand acronyms on first use.
- Avoid idioms, humour, culturally specific metaphors, flags, and unexplained
  institutional abbreviations.
- Keep one main idea per sentence and prefer active, direct language.
- Use ISO 8601-style unambiguous dates in technical records, include time zone
  where timing matters, and state units and decimal conventions.
- Keep text out of raster images. Store diagrams as editable text and provide a
  prose description of every material diagram.
- Design tables and callouts so that text expansion does not destroy meaning.
- Do not encode meaning by colour alone.
- Test Arabic and other right-to-left content for direction, ordering,
  punctuation, code fragments, and mixed-direction identifiers. W3C provides
  [language-aware HTML guidance](https://www.w3.org/TR/i18n-html-tech-lang/).
- Maintain a terminology decision log; do not silently replace a nationally
  reviewed term.

## Regional review profiles

These profiles identify planning considerations. Member-state requirements and
the actual users of a deployment remain authoritative for review scope.

### African Union contexts

The [African Union lists](https://au.int/en/about/languages) Arabic, English,
French, Portuguese, Spanish, Kiswahili, and other African languages among its
official languages. An English-only technical baseline can support coordination,
but it must not be treated as sufficient language coverage for all AU contexts.

For an AU or African member-state review:

- decide working and user-facing languages from the participating institutions;
- plan for Arabic right-to-left presentation from the beginning;
- involve local domain reviewers for national accounts terminology;
- record character-set, Office locale, number/date formatting, connectivity,
  support, and database-infrastructure assumptions by deployment;
- avoid describing one national review as “African Union compliant.”

### European Union contexts

The EU has [24 official languages](https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/languages_en).
EU guidance notes that specialized technical information may use fewer
languages depending on its target audience, while priority public content has
broader coverage ([languages on EU
websites](https://european-union.europa.eu/languages-our-websites_en)).

For an EU or EU member-state review:

- use target-user research to decide translation coverage and record the
  decision instead of assuming that English is always sufficient;
- assess legal, organizational, semantic, and technical interoperability;
- include accessibility, security/privacy, multilingualism, openness, data
  portability, and preservation as explicit concerns, reflecting the
  [European Interoperability
  Framework](https://interoperable-europe.ec.europa.eu/collection/iopeu-monitoring/european-interoperability-framework-detail);
- separate source terms, translated UI labels, statistical concepts, and data
  exchange identifiers so that semantic differences remain visible.

### ASEAN contexts

Article 34 of the [ASEAN
Charter](https://www.asean.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/2.-February-2015-The-ASEAN-Charter-18th-Reprint.pdf)
establishes English as ASEAN's working language. English is therefore a sensible
common technical review language for cross-ASEAN collaboration. It does not
remove the need to assess national terminology, user-facing language, scripts,
formats, policy, accessibility, infrastructure, and operating practice in each
participating member state.

### Other international contexts

Use the same baseline and roles for other regions. Add a local profile only
when it captures an evidenced difference. Do not duplicate the common
architecture or create region-specific forks that cannot be reconciled.

## Review completion checklist

- [ ] Baseline commit, documentation version, scope, and owner are recorded.
- [ ] Architecture claims link to evidence and distinguish unknowns.
- [ ] Deployment, database, Office, operating-system, and language assumptions
  are explicit.
- [ ] Domain, technical, database, security/privacy, operations, accessibility,
  and localization coverage is recorded, including roles not assessed.
- [ ] All blocking and major comments have an accountable disposition.
- [ ] Deferred items have an issue, owner, target, risk authority, and review
  trigger.
- [ ] Translations identify their source version and human-review status.
- [ ] Diagrams have text descriptions and do not rely on colour alone.
- [ ] Acceptance names its exact scope and does not imply regional or national
  certification beyond the reviewers' authority.
